..(Wednesday night through Monday)
Issued at 426 AM EST TUE NOV 24 2026

At the start of the long term period, a closed upper level low 
will be located over the Plains, with a well defined shortwave 
over the Gulf and a third weaker shortwave off the Atlantic Coast 
of Florida. With time, the Florida and Gulf waves will lift to the
northeast around the low, although the way that these features 
interact remains in question. The ECMWF keeps the Florida wave 
weaker and the low farther south, with the Gulf shortwave 
progressing farther east, quickly phasing with the aforementioned 
low. In contrast, the GFS keeps the Gulf shortwave slightly 
farther west than the ECMWF, eventually allowing it to become a 
more well-defined closed low itself, with weak shortwave ridging 
separating these features. With eastern Kentucky generally located
in between these two main waves, these differences will have 
implications for dynamic lift over our forecast area, which itself
will have implications for the QPF footprint associated with this
system. Regardless, confidence is high that a large scale system 
will impact the forecast area around Thanksgiving, bringing 
widespread rain to eastern Kentucky.

Rain chances will begin to increase late Wednesday night/early 
Thursday as the upper level low translates eastward toward the 
Mississippi Valley. The environment ahead of this feature will be 
anomalously moist, with a deep plume of Gulf/Atlantic moisture 
wrapping around the eastern side of the cyclone. LREF mean PW 
values increase to over 1 inch by Thursday morning, at least the 
90th percentile compared to climatology. With intense 500 mb 
height falls expected as the low continues to translate eastward, 
there will be ample forcing for rain across the forecast area, 
with PoPs peaking in the 90-100% range across the forecast area on
Thanksgiving. Winds at the surface will be northeasterly around a
deepening surface cyclone near the Carolinas, which will keep 
temperatures cool, with Thursday's highs ranging from the upper 
40s to the low 50s; thus, Thanksgiving Day looks to bring a cool 
and persistent rain, far from ideal conditions for any outdoor 
activities. Confidence in a soaking rainfall is increasing, too, 
with even the 10th percentile LREF QPF around half an inch for 
much of eastern Kentucky, while the 90th percentile (a reasonable 
high end solution) is above 2 inches. Exact QPF will again depend 
on the evolution of the system, but given such strong forcing and 
rich moisture, the LREF mean QPF, around 1.25 inches, seems 
reasonable for now. 

Overnight, winds will become increasingly westerly as the coastal
surface low lifts north and a surface cyclone begins to develop 
near the WV/OH border, with cold air wrapping around the system 
into the forecast area. Concurrently, temperatures aloft will 
begin to cool, with LREF median 850 mb temperatures falling to 
around -4C by Friday morning, although deterministic model 
guidance has trended even cooler, especially compared to previous 
days. This thermodynamic profile could allow some snow to mix into
the back side of the system, with model soundings showing an 
atmospheric column entirely below freezing early on Friday, except
for perhaps at the surface in some locations. Given this cold 
profile and trend toward cooler temperatures aloft, the 
probability for measurable snow accumulations is also increasing, 
with the LREF showing roughly a 20-40% chance of measurable snow 
accumulations on Friday and a slightly higher chance near Pine and
Black Mountains. However, before snow lovers get their hopes up, 
it is worth noting that ground temperatures are still warm, which 
will likely work against any more impactful accumulations. Even 
so, those with Friday travel plans are encouraged to keep an eye 
on future forecast updates.

With the upper level low lifting to the north by late Friday, 
height rises will overspread eastern Kentucky, with some shortwave
ridging attempting to build in the wake of this system. Model 
spread does increase significantly at this point, with some 
deterministic guidance suggesting that a second impulse could 
brush the northern portion of the forecast area late on Saturday, 
while other model runs keep eastern Kentucky in a more quasi zonal
pattern removed from northern stream energy. Chance PoPs do 
return to the forecast by Sunday as some model runs depict a cold 
front pushing through the area; however, with other model runs 
keeping eastern Kentucky under the influence of zonal flow or even
weak ridging, confidence in any additional rain remains very low 
at this time.
